title: Contest Tips and Debugging
description: Hard-won practical advice: constraints, debugging, pitfalls, and contest habits.

entries.title: Read Constraints First
entries.summary: Constraints choose the algorithm: n <= 20 invites bitmasks, 1e5 demands O(n log n), 1e9 forces math. Decide complexity before writing code.
entries.how_it_works: Map n to the affordable class: <=20 exponential, <=100 O(n^3), <=2000 O(n^2), <=1e5 O(n log n), <=1e7 O(n), huge n means O(log n) or formula. Time limit × 1e8 ops/sec budgets the constant.
entries.example:
# Constraint -> approach cheat sheet:
# n <= 20:      bitmask / meet-in-the-middle
# n <= 100:     O(n^3) Floyd-style
# n <= 2000:    O(n^2) DP
# n <= 2e5:     O(n log n) sort + structures
# n <= 1e7:     O(n) linear
# n huge:       O(log n) / math formula
pitfalls: Forgetting T test cases multiply everything
tips: Multiply everything by T (test cases)
Memory: 1e7 ints ~= 80MB in Python-weight terms
When in doubt, simulate the worst case mentally

entries.title: Brute Force First, Then Optimize
entries.summary: Write the naive solution to lock in correctness and generate test oracles, then optimize the bottleneck you can now measure. Skipping this step produces fast wrong code.
recognize: Need expected outputs for random tests
Unsure the optimized version is right
entries.how_it_works: Solve small n by definition. Keep it as a checker: fuzz random small inputs comparing brute force vs optimized. Optimize only the measured hot spot, keeping the brute force as documentation.
entries.example:
# Fuzz harness pattern:
import random
for _ in range(500):
    a = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 8))]
    assert fast(a) == brute(a), a
print('ok')
pitfalls: Deleting the brute force before final verification
Fuzzing only tiny n (include boundary sizes)
tips: Keep brute() in the file, commented as oracle
Seed the RNG for reproducible failures
Shrink failing cases by hand after fuzzing

entries.title: Killing Off-by-One Errors
entries.summary: Half-open ranges, loop invariants, and tiny examples eliminate fencepost bugs. If you can't state the invariant, you can't trust the loop.
recognize: WA on samples by exactly one
entries.how_it_works: Prefer [lo, hi) ranges uniformly. State what is true at loop entry (invariant) and check it on n=0,1,2 by hand. Trace the first and last iteration, not the middle.
entries.example:
# Invariant-first binary search (see alg.binary-search):
# invariant: answer in [lo, hi); a[lo-1] < x <= a[lo]... fix edges
# test n = 0, 1, 2 and x below/all/above before submitting
tips: Write the invariant as a comment
Test sizes 0, 1, 2 always
Half-open everywhere, no exceptions

entries.title: Overflow and Modulo Arithmetic
entries.summary: Python integers don't overflow, but subtraction under modulo goes negative and division needs modular inverses. Port carefully to and from other languages.
entries.how_it_works: Keep (a % MOD) after every op; write (x - y) % MOD (Python handles negativity, C++ doesn't). Divide via pow(a, MOD-2, MOD) for prime moduli (Fermat). Precompute factorials + inv factorials for combinations.
entries.example:
MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
fact, inv_fact = [1], [1]
# extend tables as needed, then:
# nCr = fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD * inv_fact[n - r] % MOD
def modpow(a, e=MOD - 2):
    return pow(a, e, MOD)  # Fermat inverse, MOD prime
pitfalls: (x - y) % MOD negative in C++/Java (fine in Python)
Dividing instead of multiplying by inverse
MOD not prime: Fermat doesn't apply
tips: Precompute factorials once per test file
Python // is floor, not truncation — mind negatives
Use pow(a, -1, MOD) on Python 3.8+

entries.title: Edge Case Checklist
entries.summary: Empty input, single element, all-equal, sorted/reverse, and max-size cases catch most wrong answers. Run the checklist before submitting, every time.
entries.how_it_works: Maintain a fixed list: empty, one element, two elements, all equal, sorted ascending/descending, max constraints (perf), and values at type boundaries. Feed each through the solution mentally or actually.
entries.example:
# Pre-submit checklist:
# [] / [x] / [x, y] / all-equal / sorted / reversed
# max n (time) / max values (overflow) / duplicates
# disconnected graph / single node / self-loops
tips: Automate the checklist as asserts
Empty graph/input first, always
Boundary values, not just boundary sizes

entries.title: Stress Testing Harness
entries.summary: Compare your solution against brute force on thousands of random small cases. Most hidden bugs surface within seconds of fuzzing.
recognize: Optimized version of a brute force
entries.how_it_works: Generate small random inputs, run both versions, diff. On mismatch, minimize the case (shrink n, simplify values) until the bug is obvious. Seed for reproducibility.

complexity.time: Bounded by brute force cost × trials

pitfalls: Slow brute force limiting trial count
tips: 2000 tiny cases beat 20 big ones for logic bugs
Add adversarial shapes (sorted, equal, alternating)
Keep the harness file for regression

entries.title: Recursion Limits and Stack Depth
entries.summary: Python's default recursion limit (1000) dies on path graphs and deep trees; raise it or go iterative. Know both fixes cold.
entries.how_it_works: sys.setrecursionlimit raises the Python-level cap, but C-stack segfaults lurk past ~1e5 frames. Iterative stacks with explicit state are bulletproof; threading with big stacks is the classic workaround.
entries.example:
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(1 << 20)
# For 2e5+ depth, prefer iterative:
# stack = [(root, 0)]  # (node, state)
# push (node, 1) then children with state 0 to mimic exit hooks
pitfalls: setrecursionlimit too high segfaults instead of raising
Forgetting exit-state in iterative DFS (need enter/exit markers)
Threading workaround needed on some judges
tips: Iterative DFS with (node, visited-flag) pairs
BFS avoids depth issues entirely
Test with a 2e5 path graph once, remember forever

entries.title: Modeling Problems as Graphs
entries.summary: States become nodes, moves become edges; then BFS/Dijkstra/toposort apply directly. Half of 'hard' problems are modeling plus a standard algorithm.
entries.how_it_works: Define the node as the full state (position + keys + parity...), edges as legal moves with costs. Run the matching algorithm on the implicit graph without ever building it. Multi-source BFS handles 'nearest of many'.
entries.example:
# State graph sketch (grid + keys):
# node = (r, c, keymask); moves = 4-dir + pickup
# BFS over (r, c, mask) if unweighted,
# Dijkstra if moves have costs
pitfalls: Wrong algorithm for the edge weights
tips: List every varying quantity: that's your node
Super-source/sink tricks unify multi-source/target
Time-expanded networks model waiting

entries.title: Choosing the Right Structure
entries.summary: Static + prefix queries: arrays/prefix sums. Dynamic prefix: Fenwick. General range: segment tree. Ordered: balanced BST. Match the operation mix, not the hype.
entries.how_it_works: List the operations and their frequencies: point/range, query/update, static/dynamic, ordered/unordered. Walk the decision ladder: array → prefix → Fenwick → segment tree → balanced BST → specialized (trie, suffix, persistent).
entries.example:
# Decision ladder:
# static range sum ..... prefix sums
# + point updates ....... Fenwick
# + range updates/min ... segment tree
# ordered set/map ...... sortedcontainers / BST
# strings by prefix .... trie
pitfalls: Segment tree for prefix sums (Fenwick is shorter)
tips: Write the op list first, then pick
Simplest sufficient structure wins
See ds.* entries for each rung

entries.title: BFS vs Dijkstra vs 0-1 BFS
entries.summary: Unweighted: BFS. Non-negative weights: Dijkstra. Weights {0,1}: 0-1 BFS with a deque. Picking wrong wastes time or correctness.
entries.how_it_works: BFS is Dijkstra with unit weights (queue = trivial priority). 0-1 BFS pushes 0-edges front and 1-edges back, preserving distance order without a heap. Anything negative needs Bellman-Ford.

complexity.time: BFS O(V+E); Dijkstra O((V+E) log V); 0-1 BFS O(V+E)

tips: State the weight class first, then pick
Dial's buckets generalize to small integer weights
Multi-source: push all sources at distance 0

entries.title: Bit Tricks That Pay Off
entries.summary: lowbit, popcount, power-of-two tests, and XOR properties compress common operations to one-liners. Know the five classics and their edge cases.
entries.how_it_works: x & -x isolates the lowest set bit (two's complement). x & (x-1) clears it — loop to popcount. a ^ a = 0 makes pairs cancel. 1 << k builds masks; x.bit_length() sizes tables.
tips: int.bit_count() beats bin().count()
lowbit drives Fenwick internals
Mask DP uses 1 << n sizing

entries.title: Contest Time Management
entries.summary: Read all problems first, solve in increasing difficulty, and timebox debugging. Points per minute beats pride per problem.
entries.how_it_works: Skim everything (5 min), rank by solvability, implement easiest first. Cap debugging at ~20 min: switch to stress-testing or move on. Reserve the last 10 minutes for edge cases and resubmits.
entries.example:
# Contest timeline (2h):
# 0:00-0:05  read all, rank A<B<C...
# solve easiest first, test with checklist
# 20-min debug cap per problem, then switch
# last 10 min: edge cases + frozen code review
pitfalls: No time left for easy partials
tips: First solve builds momentum — chase it
Write the checklist (tip.edge-cases) before coding
Skip and return with fresh eyes

entries.title: Upsolving After Contests
entries.summary: Re-solve failures within 48 hours while memory is fresh, then extract the pattern into your library. Rating follows upsolving volume.
entries.how_it_works: For each miss: classify (modeling, algorithm gap, bug, time). Read the editorial only to the key insight, implement yourself, then add one library entry or checklist item. Track repeats per category.
entries.example:
# Upsolve log template:
# problem / verdict / root cause class
# key insight (one line) / pattern id used
# checklist change (what will catch it next time)
tips: 48-hour rule for reimplementation
One library entry per new pattern
Review the log monthly for repeats

entries.title: Living Within Memory Limits
entries.summary: 256MB caps Python lists of ~1e7 ints in spirit but object overhead bites sooner. Use arrays, bitsets, generators, and rolling state to fit.
recognize: Storing all input when streaming works
entries.how_it_works: Python ints/objects cost ~28B+ each: prefer array('l'), numpy, or bytearray for bulk numerics. Process streaming input line by line. Roll DP dimensions; store parents only if reconstruction is needed.
pitfalls: read().split() on 100MB input (ok usually, but measure)
DP table kept whole for reconstruction nobody needs
tips: sys.stdin.buffer for speed + memory
Bitset/bytearray for boolean tables
Profile with sys.getsizeof on samples

entries.title: Designing Adversarial Tests
entries.summary: Attack your own solution: sorted, reverse, equal, alternating, and max-size inputs plus targeted tricky shapes (stars vs paths for trees). Authors hide tests here.
recognize: Passes random fuzz but WA on hidden
entries.how_it_works: Enumerate structural extremes per data type: arrays (sorted/reverse/equal/sawtooth), trees (path/star/caterpillar), graphs (complete/disconnected/line), strings (repetitive/palindrome). For greedy, actively hunt counterexamples before trusting it.
entries.example:
# Tree shape battery (n nodes):
# path:    1-2-3-...-n
# star:    1 connected to all
# binary:  heap-ordered complete tree
# caterpillar: path with one leaf per node
# run solution on all four, compare with brute
tips: Counterexample hunts belong before coding greedy
Keep a shapes file per data type
Swap roles: try to break a friend's solution

entries.title: Reading Editorials Effectively
entries.summary: Extract the single key insight, map it to a known pattern, and reimplement from the insight alone. Copying code teaches nothing; mapping patterns teaches everything.
entries.how_it_works: Read until the crux, stop, implement yourself. Name the pattern (which library entry?) and the recognition signal you missed. File both, plus the counterexample that forced the insight.
entries.example:
# Editorial extraction template:
# crux (one sentence): ...
# pattern: <library id> (or NEW)
# missed signal: ...
# minimal testcase forcing it: ...
pitfalls: Reading to the end before trying
tips: Stop at the crux, implement blind
Name the missed signal explicitly
Link the problem in your library entry notes
